title: Did Balak ever fight Israel?
summary: Joshua says Balak rose and warred against Israel. Jephthah asks, expecting the answer no, whether Balak ever fought them. The Hebrew uses the same verb in both verses.
text: Joshua 24:9 (KJV): “Balak the son of Zippor, king of Moab, arose and warred against Israel”. Judges 11:25 (KJV): “did he ever strive against Israel, or did he ever fight against them”. Hebrew (WLC) of Joshua 24:9: וַיִּלָּ֖חֶם בְּיִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל [and he fought against Israel]. Hebrew (WLC) of Judges 11:25: אִם־נִלְחֹ֥ם נִלְחַ֖ם בָּֽם [did he ever fight against them]. The Brenton Greek has παρετάξατο τῷ Ἰσραὴλ [drew up in battle order against Israel] in Joshua and πολεμῶν ἐπολέμησεν αὐτὸν [did he ever make war on him] in Judges. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/6/24/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/7/11/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOS24.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JDG11.htm.
reasoning: One speech asserts the act and the other asks a rhetorical question that denies it, about the same king and the same people, using one Hebrew verb. If the verb means armed combat in both, the speeches disagree. If Joshua’s “warred” summarises hostile action, the two can stand together: the same verse goes straight on to say Balak “sent and called Balaam” to curse.
scope: Both statements are speeches by characters making an argument, not narrator reports. A shared Hebrew root does not settle that both speakers mean the same kind of action. The KJV’s “warred” and “fight” are synonyms, so this is not tagged as a KJV departure from the Hebrew; the Hebrew is quoted only to show the wording match. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text and the Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient translation tradition. title: Joshua’s covenant assembly: Shechem or Shiloh?
summary: The KJV and the Hebrew set Joshua’s last assembly and covenant at Shechem. The Septuagint sets both at Shiloh, before the tent of God, and has no “sanctuary” in verse 26.
text: KJV Joshua 24:1: “gathered all the tribes of Israel to Shechem”; 24:25: “set them a statute and an ordinance in Shechem”; 24:26: “under an oak, that was by the sanctuary of the Lord”. Hebrew (WLC): 24:1 שְׁכֶ֑מָה [to Shechem]; 24:25 בִּשְׁכֶֽם [in Shechem]; 24:26 בְּמִקְדַּ֥שׁ יְהוָֽה [in the sanctuary of the LORD]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek): 24:1 εἰς Σηλὼ [to Shiloh]; 24:25 ἐν Σηλὼ ἐνώπιον τῆς σκηνῆς τοῦ Θεοῦ Ἰσραήλ [in Shiloh before the tent of the God of Israel]; 24:26 ὑπὸ τὴν τέρμινθον ἀπέναντι Κυρίου [under the terebinth before the Lord]. Joshua 18:1 (KJV) puts the tabernacle at Shiloh: “assembled together at Shiloh, and set up the tabernacle of the congregation there”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/6/24/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOS24.htm.
reasoning: The two text traditions name different towns for the same assembly. The Greek place agrees with where Joshua 18:1 puts the tabernacle; the Hebrew and KJV place a “sanctuary of the Lord” at Shechem without saying what it was.
scope: The passage does not say whether the “sanctuary” at Shechem was the tabernacle, a second holy place or something else, and it mentions no altar there. title: Was the altar named “Ed”?
summary: The KJV says the eastern tribes “called the altar Ed”. The Hebrew quoted here gives no name after “called”; “witness” is a common noun in the reason that follows. In the Septuagint, Joshua names the altar.
text: KJV Joshua 22:34: “called the altar Ed: for it shall be a witness between us”. Hebrew (WLC): וַֽיִּקְרְא֛וּ בְּנֵי־רְאוּבֵ֥ן וּבְנֵי־גָ֖ד לַמִּזְבֵּ֑חַ כִּ֣י עֵ֥ד הוּא֙ בֵּֽינֹתֵ֔ינוּ [and the sons of Reuben and the sons of Gad called the altar, for it is a witness between us]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek): ἐπωνόμασεν Ἰησοῦς τὸν βωμὸν [Joshua named the altar] … μαρτύριόν ἐστιν ἀναμέσον αὐτῶν [it is a testimony between them]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/6/22/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOS22.htm.
reasoning: In this Hebrew text the word for “witness” appears once, inside the explanation, and no name stands after “called the altar”. The KJV supplies “Ed” as a proper name. The Greek differs again: the namer is Joshua, not the tribes, and no name “Ed” is printed.
scope: The packaged KJV text does not mark supplied words, so it cannot show whether the translators flagged “Ed” as an addition. The Hebrew sentence is abrupt, and reading its reason clause as the name itself is a possible construction. The effect on meaning is limited to whether the altar had a proper name. title: Forty-eight Levite towns: stated totals against the names
summary: Joshua 21 names 48 Levite towns and totals 48. 1 Chronicles 6 states the same group totals, 13, 10, 13 and 12, but names 11, 8, 13 and 10. Two verses of Joshua’s list are marked as absent from the Leningrad Codex.
text: Joshua 21:41 (KJV): “forty and eight cities”; its lists name 13, 10, 13 and 12 towns. 1 Chronicles 6:60 (KJV): “All their cities throughout their families were thirteen cities”, after eleven names in verses 57–60 (Juttah and Gibeon of Joshua 21:16–17 are not there). 1 Chronicles 6:61: “ten cities”; verses 67–70 name eight (no Eltekeh or Gibbethon). 1 Chronicles 6:63: “twelve cities”; verses 77–81 name ten (two towns from Zebulun where Joshua 21:34–35 has four). The thirteen Gershonite towns are all named (6:71–76). Named total: 42. Joshua 21:25 (KJV) gives Manasseh “Gathrimmon”, the town just listed for Dan in 21:24; the Hebrew (WLC) has גַּת־רִמֹּ֖ון, the Brenton Greek has τὴν Ἰεβαθὰ [Iebatha], and 1 Chronicles 6:70 (KJV) has “Bileam”. Joshua 21:36–37, the four Reubenite towns (“four cities”): the Unicode/XML Leningrad Codex edition prints both verses with its mark [X], which its key defines as “This verse does NOT occur in the Leningrad Codex. Included for continuity of verse numbering.” The Aleppo-based consonantal edition served by bolls.life (HAC) has 43 verses in the chapter, goes from Zebulun straight to Gad, and still totals ערים שתים עשרה [twelve towns] for Merari after eight names. The Brenton Greek includes the Reubenite towns (πόλεις τέσσαρες). Fetched from https://tanach.us/Server.txt?Josh21:35-21:38, https://bolls.life/get-text/HAC/6/21/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/6/21/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOS21.htm.
reasoning: This is arithmetic inside each list. Chronicles’ stated subtotals exceed its own names by six. Joshua’s names reach 48 only with verses 36–37, which the KJV includes; without them the Hebrew names 44 and Merari has eight against a stated twelve.
scope: Different spellings or names for what may be the same town (Holon/Hilen, Ain/Ashan, Almon/Alemeth, Kibzaim/Jokmeam and others) are not counted here as contradictions. A shortfall can come from loss in copying, abbreviation or an earlier form of the list; none is shown by these texts. The G tag covers only the different town name in the Greek of 21:25. The statement about the Leningrad Codex rests on one edition’s transcription note, and the 43-verse count on how one website serves the Aleppo-based edition; a printed critical edition should be cited before either is stated as a fact about the manuscripts. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text and the Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient translation tradition. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees, and neither edition settles which reading is earlier.

title: Jacob’s land at Shechem: bought, or taken by sword and bow?
summary: Genesis 33 and Joshua 24 say Jacob bought land at Shechem. In Genesis 48:22 Jacob says he took Joseph’s extra share from the Amorite with sword and bow; the Hebrew word for that share is “shekhem”, and the Septuagint names it as Shechem.
text: Genesis 48:22 (KJV): “one portion above thy brethren, which I took out of the hand of the Amorite with my sword and with my bow”. Hebrew (WLC): שְׁכֶ֥ם אַחַ֖ד עַל־אַחֶ֑יךָ [one shekhem above your brothers]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek): δίδωμί σοι Σίκιμα ἐξαίρετον [I give you Sikima, Shechem, as a special share] … ἐν μαχαίρᾳ μου καὶ τόξῳ [with my sword and bow]. Genesis 33:19 (KJV): “he bought a parcel of a field”. Joshua 24:32 (KJV): “a parcel of ground which Jacob bought of the sons of Hamor the father of Shechem” … “it became the inheritance of the children of Joseph”. In the Brenton Greek of Joshua 24:32 the sellers are παρὰ τῶν Ἀμοῤῥαίων τῶν κατοικούντων ἐν Σικίμοις [from the Amorites living in Shechem]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/1/48/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/GEN48.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOS24.htm.
reasoning: In the Greek, one passage says Jacob took Shechem from the Amorites by weapons and another says he acquired the Shechem field from the Amorites by purchase. In the KJV the link is hidden because Genesis 48:22 reads “portion” and names no place.
scope: The Hebrew word can mean shoulder, ridge or share as well as the place name, so the KJV’s “portion” is within its range and no H tag is proposed. That Genesis 48:22 concerns the same land as Genesis 33:19 is explicit only in the Greek. Genesis 34 narrates violence at Shechem by Jacob’s sons, which Jacob condemns; whether 48:22 refers to that is not stated. title: Hornets and victory without sword or bow
summary: Joshua credits displacement to a hornet rather than Israel’s weapons, while the same speech mentions fighting. The tension depends on whether the weapon denial excludes combat or emphasizes divine agency.
text: Joshua 24:12 attributes displacement to a hornet rather than Israel’s sword or bow, referring to two Amorite kings without naming them. The same speech says the eastern Amorites and Jericho’s people fought Israel (24:8,11). Identifying the two kings as Sihon and Og follows the usage in Deuteronomy 3:8, but is an inference; verse 12 follows the western-Jordan events in verse 11. Deuteronomy 2:32-34 and 3:1-8 describes Israel striking Sihon and Og in battle while crediting divine delivery. Exodus 23:28 promises hornets. Brenton’s Greek-based English translation instead reads twelve kings at Joshua 24:12. KJV 24:12 reads “the two kings of the Amorites”, as does the Hebrew (WLC): שְׁנֵ֖י מַלְכֵ֣י הָאֱמֹרִ֑י. The Brenton Greek edition prints δώδεκα βασιλεῖς τῶν Ἀμοῤῥαίων [twelve kings of the Amorites]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/6/24/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOS24.htm.
reasoning: If the weapon denial means no Israelite fighting occurred, it conflicts with Deuteronomy’s battle reports. If it contrasts the ultimate cause of victory with self-reliance, human fighting and divine aid can coexist. The wording does not itself establish which reading is intended.
scope: The comparison does not establish whether hornet is literal, figurative, a particular natural event or a separate stage of displacement. No insect species, military chronology or independent historical event is identified. The two kings are not explicitly identified here. Brenton is a translation witness, not a critical apparatus establishing which original reading is earlier. Its twelve-kings wording limits any unqualified identification with Sihon and Og. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text and the Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient translation tradition. title: Who purchased the burial property?
summary: Joshua and Genesis name Jacob as purchaser of the Shechem land; Acts names Abraham as purchaser of a Shechem tomb. The texts do not explicitly explain the different purchaser.
text: Joshua 24:32 places Joseph’s bones in land at Shechem purchased by Jacob from Hamor’s sons; Genesis 33:19 also names Jacob. Acts 7:15-16 describes a tomb at Shechem purchased by Abraham from Hamor’s sons. Genesis 23 instead narrates Abraham purchasing the Machpelah property from Ephron near Hebron, where Genesis 50:12-13 places Jacob’s burial. In Acts 7:16, the location comes from the statement that the remains were carried to Shechem; the packaged KJV’s closing father-of-Sychem wording can refer to the person rather than the town. If the plural burial subject includes Jacob, Acts’ Shechem location also differs from Genesis 50’s Machpelah burial. If it resumes only the fathers, that particular burial-location conflict does not follow. Original-language wording: Joshua 24:32 (KJV) has “of the sons of Hamor the father of Shechem for an hundred pieces of silver”; the Hebrew (WLC) has מֵאֵ֛ת בְּנֵֽי־חֲמֹ֥ור אֲבִֽי־שְׁכֶ֖ם בְּמֵאָ֣ה קְשִׂיטָ֑ה [from the sons of Hamor, father of Shechem, for a hundred qesitah]. The Brenton Greek has other sellers and a price in animals: παρὰ τῶν Ἀμοῤῥαίων τῶν κατοικούντων ἐν Σικίμοις ἀμνάδων ἑκατὸν [from the Amorites living in Shechem, for a hundred ewe-lambs]. At Acts 7:16 the KJV ends “of the sons of Emmor the father of Sychem”. The Elzevir Textus Receptus has παρα των υιων εμμορ του συχεμ [from the sons of Emmor of Sychem; no word for “father”]. The SBL and Tischendorf editions have παρὰ τῶν υἱῶν Ἑμμὼρ ἐν Συχέμ [from the sons of Hamor in Shechem]. All three Greek editions name Abraham as the buyer. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/6/24/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOS24.htm, https://bolls.life/get-text/TR/44/7/, https://bolls.life/get-text/SBLGNT/44/7/ and https://bolls.life/get-text/TISCH/44/7/.
reasoning: The named purchaser and transaction differ. Treating Abraham and Jacob as interchangeable erases the explicit names. A separate earlier purchase or compressed family history is a possible explanation, but the compared passages do not narrate a second Abraham purchase at Shechem. Acts’ plural burial statement also needs care about which persons it includes.
scope: This establishes a textual comparison, not an archaeological identification of the tombs. Do not claim Joseph was buried at Machpelah or that every patriarch’s burial is separately documented. Original wording, narrative compression and the scope of Acts’ plural subjects require further textual study. The purchaser difference between Acts and Joshua is in the Greek New Testament editions checked, so it is not a product of English translation. Three printed Greek New Testament editions are not a manuscript apparatus; no codex is named. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text and the Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient translation tradition. title: Seventy or seventy-five family members?
summary: Exodus and Genesis give a family total of seventy; Stephen’s speech in Acts gives seventy-five. The Septuagint also reads seventy-five in Genesis 46:27 and Exodus 1:5.
text: Exodus 1:5 gives seventy descendants and notes Joseph was already in Egypt. Genesis 46:26–27 distinguishes sixty-six traveling descendants from a total household of seventy. Acts 7:14 gives seventy-five for the relatives Joseph summoned. Original-language wording: the Hebrew (WLC) has שִׁבְעִֽים [seventy] at Genesis 46:27 and שִׁבְעִ֣ים נָ֑פֶשׁ [seventy souls] at Exodus 1:5, which the KJV follows (“threescore and ten”; “seventy souls”). The Brenton Greek of Genesis 46:27 gives Joseph nine sons, not two, and a total of seventy-five: ψυχαὶ ἐννέα … ψυχαὶ ἑβδομηκονταπέντε; its Exodus 1:5 has πέντε καὶ ἑβδομήκοντα [seventy-five]. Acts 7:14 (KJV “threescore and fifteen souls”) reads ἐν ψυχαῖς ἑβδομήκοντα πέντε in the SBL and Tischendorf editions, and the same words in the Textus Receptus. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/1/46/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/2/1/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/GEN46.htm, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/EXO01.htm and https://bolls.life/get-text/SBLGNT/44/7/.
reasoning: The totals differ in all three packaged translations. The passages do not describe their counting categories in identical terms, so the numerical difference is directly visible while its explanation needs further evidence.
scope: This records an apparent textual discrepancy. Stephen’s seventy-five agrees with the Septuagint of Genesis and Exodus and disagrees with the Hebrew those KJV chapters translate. This shows where the two figures sit in the named editions; it does not show which figure is earlier or how either was counted. title: Achan’s household and individual punishment
summary: Achan’s children are included in the judgment scene, while Deuteronomy forbids executing children for a parent’s sin. The narrative does not state their individual guilt.
text: Joshua 7 begins with one named man taking prohibited spoil but attributes a trespass to Israel and connects it to the army’s defeat. Achan confesses his own action. Verse 24 lists his sons and daughters among those brought to Achor; verse 25 first describes stoning him and then uses plural objects for burning and stoning. Deuteronomy 24:16 forbids putting children to death for fathers and assigns death to each person’s own sin. Joshua 22:20 recalls that Achan did not perish alone and that wrath affected the congregation. Joshua 7:5 has already reported roughly thirty-six soldiers killed in the defeat. The later recollection confirms wider fatal consequences; it does not name each additional person or separately describe the death or guilt of each child. Verse 15 announces destruction of the offender and all he has, without separately naming the children. Brenton’s Greek-based English translation of verse 25 retains the singular stoning action but lacks the additional plural burning/stoning clause used by the packaged translations. It still includes sons and daughters in the group brought to the valley in verse 24. Original-language wording of 7:25: the KJV has “burned them with fire, after they had stoned them with stones”; the Hebrew (WLC) has וַיִּרְגְּמ֨וּ אֹתֹ֤ו כָל־יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ אֶ֔בֶן וַיִּשְׂרְפ֤וּ אֹתָם֙ בָּאֵ֔שׁ וַיִּסְקְל֥וּ אֹתָ֖ם בָּאֲבָנִֽים [all Israel stoned him … burned them … stoned them]. In the Brenton Greek, verse 25 ends with Joshua’s words and the next verse has only the singular: Καὶ ἐλιθοβόλησαν αὐτὸν λίθοις πᾶς Ἰσραὴλ [and all Israel stoned him with stones]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/6/7/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOS07.htm.
reasoning: Reading the plural action as extending to the listed family creates tension with the individual-punishment rule. The passage does not explicitly accuse the children of sharing Achan’s theft. Assuming their complicity supplies a fact not stated in this scene. Distinguishing exceptional divine judgment from ordinary legal proceedings is a proposed difference of scope, not an explicit explanation of each family member’s responsibility here. The retrospective statement therefore cannot settle the household question by itself: the earlier military deaths are also part of the narrative consequences.
scope: The final actions do not itemize each victim, so do not claim the text separately describes every child’s execution. The household-inclusive reading is a qualified interpretation of the listed group and plural wording. The collective military consequences and the execution rule are related but not identical kinds of responsibility. No independent historical occurrence or geological mechanism is established. The plural-action argument depends on the longer wording in the packaged editions; Brenton illustrates a different textual tradition without settling priority or the fate of every family member. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text and the Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient translation tradition.
